newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers' roadblocks in place for 12th day.
newsitem.headline: French truckers' roadblocks in place for 12th day.

text.p: French truckers planned to keep their roadblocks in place for a 12th day on Friday, in a protest sending shockwaves across Europe's economies.
Employers and unions were due to meet at 9.30 a.m. (0830 GMT) to ratify deals on early retirement and working conditions reached on Thursday before talks broke down over wage demands.
An unrelated blockade by truckers in Denmark appeared to have ended late on Thursday, however.
As the French strikers' stranglehold bit deeper and fuel rationing spread, there was little sign of how a wide gap between their demands and the employers' offer would be bridged.
Unions demand pay hikes amounting to an average 23 percent. Employers offer a one percent real pay rise and a 1,500 franc ($300) one-time bonus.
"I think (the blockade) will go on for a while," said Roger Poletti of the Force Ouvriere (FO) union. "The truckers' determination is untouched."
Yet unions signalled willingness to resume negotiations, and bosses said that while they could not increase their offer, they would be flexible in re-arranging its terms.
Employers' spokesman Rene Petit said raising the pay offer would plunge many haulage companies into dire financial straits.
Transport Minister Bernard Pons said he could not impose a pay deal. But he said employers had left the door open to an accord and suggested they could offer a second one-time bonus.
"I think there will be advances in the next hours," he said.

Pons said "very positive results were obtained" before the talks broke down over pay, including the right for truckers to retire at 55 after 25 years at the wheel, changes on sick pay and travel expenses, and a ban on trucks driving at weekends.

He said the government would provide guarantees that the deals would be implemented, to overcome the distrust of truckers who say many companies failed to respect agreements reached after a similar blockade four years ago.
Pons said unions and employers would try to define working hours for drivers and he would propose to settle the delicate issue by decree if they failed to agree quickly.
Truckers say they often work more than 200 hours a month, with many hours unpaid as they wait for loading and unloading.

Radio reports said two truckers were injured as tempers frayed and a motorist forced his way through a roadblock near Chalon-sur-Saone. A German trucker was hit by a stone and seriously hurt in the same area earlier this week.
The strike, in the crucial pre-Christmas commercial period, has cost European food and haulage industries tens of millions of dollars a day, prompting protests from France's neighbours.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe said the dispute would soon have dire economic consequences and had to be settled urgently.
But he ruled out using force to clear the barricades set across some 250 roads, around 150 fuel depots and at the country's 13 oil refineries.
Petrol rationing spread and about 5,000 of 18,000 petrol stations were either dry or feeling shortages.
The roadblocks have forced the closures of some factories for lack of supplies and cut deliveries of perishable goods ranging from fish to fruit and flowers.
Farmers reported shortages of animal feed as grain shipments were hit and the strike was also disrupting mail.
The blockade stranded up to 14,000 Spanish trucks and idled about 90 percent of Portugal's total truck fleet. Belgian ports were clogged by British-bound lorries avoiding France.
Strikers briefly relaxed their blockade of the Channel port of Calais on Thursday night to let hundreds of stranded British trucks get on ferries for home.
Danish truckers late on Thursday voted to end immediately their four-day blockade of seaports and the land border with Germany, Danish news agency Ritzau said.
The agency said after a mass meeting drivers they began moving towards their vehicles.
